summary: This proposed standard defines a rendezvous extension for the Host Identity Protocol, extending HIP and its registration extension to start communication through rendezvous servers. These servers improve reachability when HIP nodes are multihomed or mobile.

plainLanguage.summary: A rendezvous server is a fixed relay that HIP hosts register with, so a peer can reach a host whose IP address has changed. The peer sends its first packet to the relay, and the relay forwards it to the address the host last registered.

subtitle: How a HIP host that keeps changing its IP address stays reachable through a fixed relay.

tldr.problem: A HIP host that moves or switches networks often cannot be found by peers who do not yet know where it is.
tldr.mechanism: The host registers its Host Identity Tags and its current IP addresses with a rendezvous server. A peer sends the first HIP packet to that server, which rewrites the destination address and forwards it to the address on file.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8004 obsoletes RFC 5204, and its only other change was updating references to the revised HIP specifications. The relay must sign any address it rewrites, so the original sender stays verifiable.

today: RFC 8004 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5204, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The document itself records one change from the version it replaces: its references to the HIP specifications were updated.

sections.title: Why a Rendezvous Server
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) lets a host be known by a stable cryptographic name rather than by its IP address. The HIP architecture introduces a rendezvous mechanism to help a HIP node contact a node that moves often. The mechanism involves a third party, the rendezvous server (RVS), which serves as the initial contact point for its clients.

The clients of an RVS are HIP nodes that use the HIP Registration Extension to register their Host Identity Tag (HIT) to IP address mappings with the RVS. After that registration, other HIP nodes can start a base exchange using the IP address of the RVS instead of the current IP address of the node they want to reach. The clients of an RVS therefore become reachable at the RVS's IP address, and the RVS relays the exchange so that it can complete.
sections.plainLanguage: A HIP host can be found by a stable name even when its IP address changes. A rendezvous server holds the current address and forwards first contact, so peers do not need to know where the host is right now.

sections.title: Rendezvous Roles and Terms
sections.content:
Besides the terminology of the HIP specification and the HIP Registration Extension, this document defines four terms.

  • Rendezvous service: the service an RVS offers, relaying some of the arriving base exchange packets between the Initiator and the Responder.
  • Rendezvous server (RVS): a HIP registrar that provides rendezvous service.
  • Rendezvous client: a HIP requester that has registered for rendezvous service at an RVS.
  • Rendezvous registration: the HIP registration for rendezvous service, established between an RVS and a rendezvous client.

In this specification the client of an RVS is always the Responder. There might be reasons to allow a client to start a base exchange through its own RVS, such as NAT and firewall traversal, but this specification does not address such scenarios and they should be specified in other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names four roles: the server that relays packets, the client that registers with it, the service the server offers, and the registration that links the two together.

sections.title: Relaying the Base Exchange
sections.content:
Without a rendezvous server, the Initiator sends the I1 packet of the HIP base exchange directly to the Responder's IP address, and the exchange continues with R1, I2 and R2.

With an RVS, the Initiator sends the I1 either to one of the Responder's IP addresses, if it knows one from DNS or other means, or to one of the Responder's RVSs. In the latter case the Initiator obtains the RVS's address from the Responder's DNS record, which the Responder publishes with the HIP DNS resource record type. The RVS notices that the HIT in the arriving I1 is not its own, checks its current registrations, finds that the HIT belongs to the Responder, and relays the I1 to the registered IP address. The Responder then completes the base exchange without further assistance from the RVS, by sending R1 directly to the Initiator's IP address as obtained from the I1 packet.

The Responder is assumed to have registered its HITs and current IP addresses with the RVS earlier, using the HIP Registration Extension. When a HIP node has registered with an RVS, it should record the RVS's IP address in its DNS record.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a HIP client sends its first packet straight to the other host. With a rendezvous server, the client sends that first packet to the server instead. The server looks up the destination name in its records and forwards the packet to the address on file. The reply then travels directly between the two hosts.

sections.title: Registering With a Rendezvous Server
sections.content:
Before an RVS relays HIP packets to a rendezvous client, the client must register with it to receive rendezvous service, using the HIP Registration Extension. The exchange follows the shape of a HIP base exchange: the client sends I1, the server answers with R1 carrying a REG_INFO parameter, the client sends I2 carrying a REG_REQ parameter, and the server replies with R2 carrying a REG_RES parameter.

The same extension is used to tell the RVS about a change in the client's location. The extensions described here allow a HIP node to register with an RVS for rendezvous service and to notify the RVS of changes to its current location.
sections.plainLanguage: A host has to register with the server before the server will forward anything for it. The registration follows the usual HIP handshake, and it is the step that sets up the keys used later to protect packets between host and server.

sections.title: The Three New HIP Parameters
sections.content:
The RVS works with three new parameters in the HIP header, each identified by a type code.

  • FROM, type 65498, length 16: an IPv6 address or an IPv4-in-IPv6 format IPv4 address. The RVS must add it whenever it rewrites the source address of a HIP packet, and must append it after any FROM parameters that are already present.
  • RVS_HMAC, type 65500, variable length: a hashed message authentication code computed over the HIP packet, excluding the RVS_HMAC parameter and any parameters that follow it. It is keyed with the HIP integrity key established when the rendezvous registration happened. Its only difference from the HMAC parameter of the HIP specification is the type code, which places it after the FROM parameter.
  • VIA_RVS, type 65502, variable length: an IPv6 address or an IPv4-in-IPv6 format IPv4 address. After a Responder receives a relayed I1, it must append a newly created VIA_RVS parameter at the end of the R1 packet, holding the IP address of the RVS that relayed the I1. The goal is to let operators diagnose problems met while establishing a HIP association through an RVS.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new fields travel in the HIP header. One records the original sender's address when the server replaces it. One carries a code computed from a shared key that shows the packet was not altered on the way. One names the server that relayed the packet, so operators can trace a failing connection.

sections.title: Packet Processing Rules
sections.content:
When an RVS relays an inbound I1 packet that carries one of the client's HITs, it rewrites the IP header. It replaces the destination IP address with one of the IP addresses of the owner of the HIT, the rendezvous client, and must recompute the IP checksum accordingly. Because of ingress filtering on the path from the RVS to the client, an RVS should also replace the source IP address with one of its own, chosen according to the relevant IPv4 and IPv6 specifications. Because that replacement conceals the Initiator's address, the RVS must append a FROM parameter holding the original source address, and that parameter must be integrity protected by an RVS_HMAC keyed with the corresponding rendezvous registration integrity key.

The RVS should verify the checksum of an I1 packet before modifying it. After the modification it must recompute the checksum using the updated HIP header, which may include new FROM and RVS_HMAC parameters, and a pseudo-header containing the updated source and destination IP addresses. This lets the Responder validate the checksum of the I1 packet as it arrives, without having to parse any FROM parameters.

An RVS that receives an I1 whose destination HIT is not its own consults its registration database for a rendezvous registration established by the HIT owner. If it finds an appropriate registration it relays the packet to the registered IP address; if it does not, it drops the packet. An incoming opportunistic I1, which has a NULL destination HIT, should be interpreted as an I1 addressed to the RVS itself and should not be relayed to a client. A rendezvous client receiving an I1 must validate any RVS_HMAC parameter; if it cannot be verified the packet should be dropped, and it must be dropped when a FROM parameter is present. A client acting as Responder should drop opportunistic I1s that include a FROM parameter, because that shows the packet has been relayed.

When a Responder replies to an I1 relayed through an RVS, it must append a VIA_RVS parameter with the IP addresses of the traversed RVSs to the regular R1 header. The Initiator checks that it sent an I1 to the originator of the R1. For a relayed exchange this check should be based on HITs only, and if IP addresses are also checked, the source IP address must be checked against the IP address included in the VIA_RVS parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The server rewrites the address on the first packet so it reaches the right host, then recomputes the checksum. It may also replace the sender's address to get past network filtering, and then it adds the original address in a field protected by a shared key. If no matching registration exists, the server drops the packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document argues that the extensions it describes do not add new threats to HIP. It notes that it is hard to cover the whole scope of threats introduced by RVSs, because their presence has implications at both the IP layer and the HIP layer. The extensions might allow redirection, amplification and reflection attacks at the IP layer, as well as attacks on the HIP layer itself, for example man-in-the-middle attacks against the HIP base exchange.

An Initiator that already knows the Responder's host identity when it first contacts the Responder through an RVS has a means to verify the signatures in the HIP base exchange, which protects against man-in-the-middle attacks. An Initiator without that prior knowledge, an opportunistic Initiator, can hardly be defended against, because the public keys exchanged cannot be authenticated. The only approach would be to require an R1 answering an opportunistic I1 to come from the same IP address that originally sent the I1, which retains a level of security equivalent to what exists in the Internet today. For reasons of simplicity, this specification does not allow the establishment of a HIP association through an RVS in an opportunistic manner.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay can be misused to redirect or amplify traffic, and a relay sitting in the middle of a handshake can try to take the place of one of the hosts. If the initiator already knows the identity of the host it wants to reach, the signatures in the handshake expose the attack. If it does not, there is no defence, so this document does not allow that case at all.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 5204, which this document obsoletes, made the following definitions and reservations in the Parameter Types subregistry under Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Parameters: 65498 for FROM with a length of 16, 65500 for RVS_HMAC with a variable length, and 65502 for VIA_RVS with a variable length. References to RFC 5204 in that subregistry have been replaced by references to this document.

The same document made one reservation in the Registration Types subregistry under Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Parameters: the value 1 for RENDEZVOUS. References to RFC 5204 in that subregistry have also been replaced by references to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The document assigns the numbers for three new header fields and for one new kind of registration, taking over the registrations made by the version it replaces.
